title: Abu Bakr as-Siddiq
subtitle: The companion in the cave, the first caliph
sources: Qur'an 9:40 — 'as one of two, when they were in the cave'
Sahih al-Bukhari 3661 — the Prophet ﷺ tells the people to leave his companion Abu Bakr alone
Sahih al-Bukhari 3905 — the Hijrah with Abu Bakr, including the cave
Sahih al-Bukhari 1400 — his caliphate and the wars of apostasy
Sahih al-Bukhari 3653 — Abu Bakr in the cave: 'what do you think of two whose third is Allah'
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 249-250 and 318 (his Islam and call; Bilal and the six he freed), read on shamela.ws, book 23833

chapters.heading: The One Who Never Hesitated
chapters.body: When Abu Bakr accepted Islam he openly declared it and called others to Allah and His Messenger (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 249); those who accepted through his call included Uthman ibn Affan and al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam (p. 250). When Bilal was laid on his back at midday in the valley of Makkah with a great rock on his chest, saying only 'Ahad, Ahad', Abu Bakr offered Umayya ibn Khalaf a stronger black slave of his own in exchange and then freed Bilal; Ibn Hisham lists six whom he freed on Islam, among them Amir ibn Fuhayra, Umm Ubays and Zunayra (p. 318). When the hijrah came he was chosen as the Prophet's companion. In the cave, Abu Bakr said that if one of the pursuers looked down at his feet he would see them, and the Prophet ﷺ answered: what do you think of two whose third is Allah? (Sahih al-Bukhari 3653); the Qur'an keeps the words 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us' (9:40). When others spoke harshly of Abu Bakr, the Prophet ﷺ told the people to leave his companion alone (Sahih al-Bukhari 3661). After the Prophet ﷺ died he became caliph and fought those who withheld the zakat (Sahih al-Bukhari 1400).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Abu Bakr spent everything he had freeing people he didn't know. What would you empty your account for?

title: Umar ibn al-Khattab
subtitle: Al-Faruq — the one who separated truth from falsehood
sources: The Prophet's ﷺ dream of Umar's palace in Paradise — Sahih al-Bukhari 3680
History (not a hadith): Umar's introduction of the Hijri calendar — Not yet scholar-reviewed
Sahih Muslim 2398 — 'if there were inspired ones in this ummah, Umar would be one of them'
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3686 — 'were there a prophet after me, it would be Umar' (hasan — Darussalam)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3863 — Ibn Mas'ud: 'we have been powerful since Umar embraced Islam'
Sahih al-Bukhari 3700 — Umar stabbed during the prayer by the slave of al-Mughira
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 343-344 (Umar's conversion account, first part), read on shamela.ws, book 23833

chapters.heading: Strength Given to the Truth
chapters.body: He set out, girded with his sword, to kill the Prophet ﷺ (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 343). Nu'aym ibn Abdullah, a man of his own clan who had become Muslim in secret, told him to look first to his sister and her husband: Khabbab used to visit Fatima bint al-Khattab to teach her the Qur'an, and her husband Sa'id ibn Zayd was also a secret Muslim (pp. 343-344). Umar struck his sister and wounded her, and a page headed 'Ta-Ha' was in the house (p. 344); the text then runs on to a page not read for this audit. Ibn Mas'ud said: 'We have been powerful since Umar embraced Islam' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3863). The Prophet ﷺ saw in a dream a palace in Paradise that he was told was Umar's (Sahih al-Bukhari 3680), and said of him: were there a prophet after me, it would be Umar (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3686 — hasan, Darussalam). At the end of his caliphate he was stabbed during the prayer by the slave of al-Mughira (Sahih al-Bukhari 3700). Other reports about him, not checked here and not from the six books: the Prophet's dua for Islam to be strengthened through Umar, his night rounds of Madinah, the saying about a mule stumbling on the banks of the Euphrates, the fixing of the Hijri calendar, the garrison cities and the registers of the conquered lands.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Umar carried responsibility for a mule on the Euphrates. What responsibility are you avoiding that is actually yours?

title: Uthman ibn Affan
subtitle: Who equipped the army of hardship and had the Qur'an copied
sources: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3701 — his gift for the army of hardship (hasan — Darussalam)
Qur'an 33:23 — 'among the believers are men true to what they promised Allah' (revealed at the pledge of ar-Ridwan)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 — Uthman and the copying of the Qur'an
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 p. 323 (the first emigration to Abyssinia), read on shamela.ws, book 23833

chapters.heading: The Modest Millionaire
chapters.body: Uthman ibn Affan emigrated to Abyssinia in the first emigration with his wife Ruqayyah, the Prophet's ﷺ daughter (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 323). When the army of Tabuk lacked supplies, he gave a thousand dinars to equip it (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3701 — hasan, Darussalam). As caliph he had the Qur'an copied from the manuscripts kept by Hafsa: Hudhayfa had been alarmed at the differences in recitation, Zayd ibn Thabit, Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn al-As and Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith made the copies, one was sent to each province, and the other fragments and manuscripts were ordered burnt; where the scribes differed from Zayd they were to write in the dialect of Quraysh, since the Qur'an was revealed in it (Sahih al-Bukhari 4987). Other reports about him, not checked here and not from the six books: that he took the title Dhun-Nurayn through marrying a second daughter, Umm Kulthum, after Ruqayyah's death; and that he was besieged in his house and killed there while forbidding his household to fight and reading the Qur'an.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Uthman equipped an army in secret and asked no credit. When you give, do you need the receipt?

title: Ali ibn Abi Talib
subtitle: Among the first to believe — a young cousin of the Prophet ﷺ and the fourth caliph
sources: Sahih Muslim 2404 — 'you are to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me'
Sahih al-Bukhari 2942 — the banner at Khaybar and Ali's eyes
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 245, 483 and 625 (Ali's Islam; the bed; the Badr duels), read on shamela.ws, book 23833

chapters.heading: The Boy Who Slept in the Prophet's Bed
chapters.body: Ibn Ishaq says Ali was the first male to believe in the Messenger of Allah, praying with him at the age of ten, and that he had been in the Prophet's ﷺ care before Islam (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 245). On the night of the hijrah, with Quraysh gathered at the door, the Prophet ﷺ told Ali to sleep in his bed under his green Hadrami cloak, saying nothing they disliked would reach him; in Ibn Hisham, when they rose in the morning Ali got up from the bed and they said, 'The one who told us was telling the truth' (p. 483). He is said to have returned the trusts left with the Prophet ﷺ before following him; that detail is not on the pages read. 'You are to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me' (Sahih Muslim 2404). At Badr, after the Ansar youths came forward, Quraysh asked for their equals; the Prophet ﷺ sent Ubayda, Hamza and Ali, and Ali killed al-Walid ibn Utba and then helped Hamza finish Utba (Ibn Hisham, p. 625). At Khaybar the Prophet ﷺ said he would give the banner to a man at whose hands Allah would grant victory; Ali had sore eyes, the Prophet ﷺ spat in them and they were cured at once, and he was given the banner (Sahih al-Bukhari 2942). That his sermons were later collected for their eloquence is a claim whose attribution is disputed; it was not checked here.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Ali slept in the Prophet's bed knowing swords were coming. What has your loyalty ever cost you?

title: Hamza ibn Abdul-Muttalib
subtitle: The lion of Allah and His Messenger
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 1 pp. 291-292 (shamela.ws/book/23833/314-315); vol. 2 pp. 95-96, 99, 122 (shamela.ws/book/23833/832, 833, 836, 859)
Qur'an 16:126 — the verse said to have answered the mutilation

chapters.heading: The Uncle Who Became the Lion
chapters.body: Ibn Hisham tells that Abu Jahl met the Prophet ﷺ at al-Safa, insulted him, attacked his religion and belittled his message, and the Prophet ﷺ did not answer him. When Hamza heard of it he struck Abu Jahl with his bow and wounded his head; when men of Banu Makhzum rose to defend Abu Jahl, Abu Jahl himself told them to leave Hamza alone, because he had cursed Hamza's nephew. Hamza then settled in Islam and in following the Prophet ﷺ. Quraysh saw that the Prophet ﷺ had gained strength and protection and that Hamza would defend him, and they held back from some of the harm they had been doing him. At Uhud, Ibn Hisham lists Hamza among the Muhajirun who were martyred and says Wahshi, a slave of Jubayr ibn Mut'im, killed him. The Prophet ﷺ found him in the bottom of the valley with his belly torn open to the liver and his nose and ears cut off. Ibn Hisham reports that the Prophet ﷺ swore that if Allah gave him the upper hand over Quraysh he would mutilate thirty of their men (the number in this book is thirty), and that Ibn Ishaq, from Ibn Abbas through a narrator he does not name, says Allah then revealed the verse permitting an equal response while praising patience (16:126): the Prophet ﷺ pardoned, was patient, and forbade mutilation. The same book says that when he passed a house of the Ansar and heard weeping for their dead, he wept and said Hamza had no one to weep for him, and that Gabriel told him Hamza is recorded in the seven heavens as the Lion of Allah and the Lion of His Messenger.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Hamza used his strength the day he heard his nephew insulted. What strength of yours is waiting for the right cause?

title: Bilal ibn Rabah
subtitle: The caller of Islam — the muezzin whose footsteps were heard in Paradise
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 1 p. 318 (shamela.ws/book/23833/341); vol. 2 p. 413 (shamela.ws/book/23833/1150)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1149 — Bilal's footsteps ahead in Paradise (Abu Hurayrah)

chapters.heading: Ahad, Under the Stone
chapters.body: Ibn Hisham says Bilal was the slave of Umayya ibn Khalaf of Banu Jumah, and that Umayya and others of Banu Jumah laid a heavy rock on his chest in the heat of midday in Makkah and demanded that he give up Muhammad ﷺ and worship al-Lat and al-Uzza. His answer was one word, repeated: Ahad, Ahad — One, One. Abu Bakr passed by and told Umayya to fear Allah; Umayya answered that Abu Bakr had corrupted Bilal and could rescue him himself. Abu Bakr offered a stronger black slave of his own in exchange, Umayya accepted, and Abu Bakr took Bilal and freed him — an exchange, not a purchase. On the day Makkah was conquered, Ibn Hisham says, the Prophet ﷺ entered the Kaaba with Bilal and ordered him to call the adhan. The Prophet ﷺ once asked Bilal at Fajr to tell him of the deed in Islam he hoped most from, because he had heard Bilal's footsteps ahead of him in Paradise; Bilal answered that he knew of no deed beyond this — whenever he made wudu, by day or night, he prayed as much as was written for him to pray (Sahih al-Bukhari 1149).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Bilal's one word under a boulder became the adhan over the Kaaba. What is your one word that could outlive your circumstances?

title: Salman al-Farsi
subtitle: The seeker who passed from teacher to teacher until he found the Prophet ﷺ
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 1 pp. 214-221 (shamela.ws/book/23833/237-244); vol. 2 p. 219 (shamela.ws/book/23833/956)

chapters.heading: From Fire-Keeper to Free Man
chapters.body: Ibn Hisham gives Salman's story in his own words. He was a Persian from Isfahan, from a village called Jay, whose father was the village headman and kept him closely confined at home; he gave himself to the Magian religion until he became keeper of the sacred fire. Sent to the family farm, he passed a church, heard Christians praying and liked their worship, and was told their religion came from Syria. He slipped off the shackle his father had put on his leg and left with a caravan of Christian merchants; in Syria he asked for the most learned man and was sent to the bishop. From there he passed from teacher to teacher — Mosul, Nasibin, Amorion — each pointing him to the next as he died. The last told him a prophet was coming in Arabia, who would settle in a land between two lava fields with palm trees, would accept gifts but not charity, and would bear the seal of prophethood between his shoulders. Merchants of Kalb took him toward Arabia but at Wadi al-Qura betrayed him and sold him as a slave to a Jewish man; later a cousin of his master, of Banu Qurayza, bought him and took him to Madinah, and he knew the town from his teacher's description. At Quba he brought food as charity and the Prophet ﷺ told his companions to eat but did not eat; in Madinah he brought food as a gift and the Prophet ﷺ ate. At Baqi' al-Gharqad he looked for the seal; the Prophet ﷺ uncovered his back, and Salman kissed it and wept. The Prophet ﷺ told him to make a contract for his freedom — to plant and tend 300 palm trees and pay 40 uqiyya — and the companions helped with palm shoots; a gold piece the size of a hen's egg came from a mine, the Prophet ﷺ had Salman take it, and he weighed out the forty uqiyya and was freed. Ibn Hisham says his slavery kept him from Badr and Uhud; he was at the Trench as a free man. There, in Salman's own account, a rock in his part of the trench would not break; the Prophet ﷺ took the pickaxe from him and struck it, and a light flashed under the pickaxe each time. The Prophet ﷺ explained the flashes as Allah opening Yemen, then Syria and the West, then the East. (Ibn Hisham also has a section on Salman's counsel to dig the trench; its text was not read for this audit, so it is not repeated here.)
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Salman crossed lands and masters to find the truth, and kept looking after each loss. What would you be willing to cross to find it?

title: Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah
subtitle: The trustworthy one of this ummah — who pulled the helmet rings from the Prophet's ﷺ cheek at Uhud
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 2 p. 80 (shamela.ws/book/23833/817)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3744 — the trustworthy one of this ummah (Anas)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3790 — the virtues of Abu Ubaidah, Mu'adh and others (sahih — Darussalam)

chapters.heading: The Pull of the Rings
chapters.body: Ibn Hisham, telling what the Prophet ﷺ suffered at Uhud, says one of his lower front teeth was broken, his lower lip was wounded by Utba ibn Abi Waqqas, and Ibn Qami'a struck his cheek so that two rings of his helmet lodged in it. In a report from Aisha, from Abu Bakr, Abu Ubaidah pulled the rings out, and both his front teeth fell out. (The page says he pulled them out; it does not say how.) The Prophet ﷺ said of him that every nation has a trustworthy one, and the trustworthy one of this ummah is Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah (Sahih al-Bukhari 3744, from Anas; also Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3790, sahih per Darussalam).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Abu Ubaidah gave his own teeth to spare the Prophet's ﷺ pain. What small sacrifice of yours would mean more than a grand one?

title: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas
subtitle: The first to shoot an arrow in the path of Allah
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3728 — Sa'd: the first of the Arabs to shoot an arrow for Allah
Sahih al-Bukhari 4055 — 'Shoot, may my father and mother be ransomed for you'
Sahih Muslim 1748 (sunnah.com 1748c) — Sa'd and his mother; Qur'an 29:8, 31:15
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3747 — Sa'd among the ten given glad tidings of Paradise (sahih — Darussalam)

chapters.heading: The Arrow and the Mother
chapters.body: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas said: “I was the first among the Arabs to shoot an arrow for Allah's cause” (Sahih al-Bukhari 3728). At Uhud the Prophet ﷺ drew an arrow from his quiver for him and said: shoot, may my father and mother be ransomed for you (Sahih al-Bukhari 4055). His trial was at home. Sa'd reports in Sahih Muslim that his mother swore she would not speak to him until he gave up his faith, and went three days without food or drink until she fainted; the verses cited in that report are 29:8 and 31:15, telling him not to obey his parents in associating anything with Allah while keeping good company with them in this world. 'And We have enjoined upon man [care] for his parents ... But if they endeavor to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them' (31:14-15). The Prophet ﷺ counted him among the ten given the glad tidings of Paradise (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3747 — sahih, Darussalam).

familyQuestion: Sa'd's mother starved herself to pull him from Islam and the Qur'an answered his case. What do you do when the people you love most pull against your faith?

title: Talha and Zubayr
subtitle: Talha, whose hand was paralysed shielding the Prophet ﷺ — and az-Zubayr, at his side at Uhud
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 2 pp. 80, 83, 86 (shamela.ws/book/23833/817, 820, 823)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3724 — Talha's paralysed hand
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3747 — Talha and Zubayr among the ten given glad tidings of Paradise (sahih — Darussalam)

chapters.heading: The Living Shields
chapters.body: Ibn Hisham, in his account of Uhud, says that after the Prophet ﷺ fell into a pit Talha ibn Ubaydullah lifted him to his feet, and that Talha sat beneath him until he stood on the rock; the same pages give the saying that whoever wishes to see a martyr walking on the earth should look at Talha. Both Talha and az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam are named among those who escorted the Prophet ﷺ up to the mountain pass. Qais ibn Abi Hazim said he saw Talha's hand — the one he had used to shield the Prophet ﷺ — paralysed (Sahih al-Bukhari 3724; the page does not name the battle). Both are among the ten given the glad tidings of Paradise (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3747 — sahih, Darussalam).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Talha's hand hung useless from shielding the Prophet ﷺ. What are you willing to take a hit for?

title: Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf
subtitle: The merchant of the ummah — who asked only: show me the market
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 2048 — Abd al-Rahman and Sa'd ibn al-Rabi'; the market, the dowry, the wedding feast
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3747 — among the ten given glad tidings of Paradise (sahih — Darussalam)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3749 — the Prophet's ﷺ prayer for Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf (hasan — Darussalam)

chapters.heading: Commerce as Worship
chapters.body: When Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf emigrated to Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ paired him as a brother with Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', one of the richest of the Ansar. Sa'd offered to share his property with him and to release one of his two wives so that Abd al-Rahman could marry her. Abd al-Rahman refused and asked only: where is the market? Sa'd showed him the market of Qaynuqa'. The next day he traded there and made a profit in dried curd and butter, and kept going back. A few days later he appeared with a yellow trace on him; the Prophet ﷺ asked whether he had married, and he said yes, an Ansari woman, with a dowry of gold equal in weight to a date-stone. The Prophet ﷺ told him to hold a wedding feast, even with a single sheep (Sahih al-Bukhari 2048). The Prophet ﷺ named him among the ten given the glad tidings of Paradise (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3747 — sahih, Darussalam), and prayed for him (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3749 — hasan, Darussalam).

familyQuestion: Abdur-Rahman was offered half of everything and asked only for the market. What honest door could you ask for instead of a handout?

title: Sa'id ibn Zayd and Zayd ibn Harithah
subtitle: The tenth of the ten — and the beloved freedman whom Allah named
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 1 pp. 247-249, 343 (shamela.ws/book/23833/270-272, 366)
Qur'an 33:5 and 33:37
Sahih al-Bukhari 1246 — the Prophet ﷺ tells of Zayd, Ja'far and Ibn Rawaha at Mu'tah (Anas)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3747 — Sa'id ibn Zayd among the ten given glad tidings of Paradise (sahih — Darussalam)

chapters.heading: Two Names, Two Honors
chapters.body: Ibn Hisham reports that horsemen of Banu al-Qayn seized Zayd ibn Harithah as a child and sold him at the market of Hubasha (a footnote gives his age as about eight); Hakim ibn Hizam brought him from Syria among a group of slaves; Khadijah chose him from the boys offered to her and gave him to the Prophet ﷺ, who freed him and adopted him before the revelation. His father Haritha grieved for him and came, with Zayd's uncle, to the Prophet ﷺ to ask for him back. The Prophet ﷺ let Zayd choose, Zayd chose to stay with him, and the Prophet ﷺ declared before the leaders of Quraysh that Zayd was his son and heir. He was called Zayd ibn Muhammad until 33:5 was revealed: 'Call them by [the names of] their fathers; it is more just in the sight of Allah' (33:5), and Zayd is named in 33:37. Telling the battle of Mu'tah, the Prophet ﷺ said Zayd took the flag and was killed, then Ja'far, then Ibn Rawaha, and his eyes were full of tears (Sahih al-Bukhari 1246). Sa'id ibn Zayd was the tenth of the ten given glad tidings of Paradise (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3747 — sahih, Darussalam). In Ibn Hisham's account of Umar's conversion, Umar's sister Fatima bint al-Khattab and her husband Sa'id ibn Zayd had become Muslim and were hiding it from Umar, and Khabbab used to visit Fatima to teach her the Qur'an; how that story ends was not read for this chapter.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Zayd chose the Prophet ﷺ over his own father, then carried his father's name forever. What does that teach about love that costs nothing of honor?

title: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud
subtitle: The first to recite the Qur'an aloud to Quraysh at the Maqam
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 1 pp. 314-315 (shamela.ws/book/23833/337-338)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3808 — take the Qur'an from four, Ibn Mas'ud first (Masruq)

chapters.heading: The Voice at the Maqam
chapters.body: Ibn Hisham tells that the companions of the Prophet ﷺ said Quraysh had never heard the Qur'an openly, and Abdullah ibn Mas'ud volunteered to make them hear it. They feared for him and wanted someone with a clan to protect him; he said Allah would protect him. In the forenoon, while Quraysh sat in their gatherings, he stood at the Maqam and recited aloud — the basmala, then the opening of Surat al-Rahman — and kept reciting while Quraysh asked one another what he was saying. They turned on him and struck his face. He went back to his companions with the marks of the blows, said the enemies of Allah were no easier for him than they were at that moment, and offered to do it again the next day; they told him it was enough, he had made them hear what they dislike. The Prophet ﷺ told the people to take the Qur'an from four, naming Ibn Mas'ud first, then Salim, Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ubayy ibn Ka'b (Sahih al-Bukhari 3808, from Masruq).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Ibn Mas'ud volunteered though his companions feared for him. When did you last volunteer first for something costly?

title: Ammar ibn Yasir
subtitle: The son of Sumayya — whose family was told: be patient, your promise is Paradise
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 1 pp. 319-320 (shamela.ws/book/23833/342-343)
Qur'an 16:106 — 'except for one who is forced, while his heart is secure in faith'
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3798 — the Prophet's ﷺ welcome of Ammar (hasan — Darussalam)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2812 — Ammar and the building of the mosque (Abu Sa'id)

chapters.heading: Forced Words, Secure Heart
chapters.body: Ibn Hisham says Banu Makhzum would bring Ammar and his father out and punish them, and that the Prophet ﷺ passed them as they were tortured in Makkah's midday heat and, in a report that reached the author, said: patience, family of Yasir, your promise is Paradise. Of Ammar's mother Sumayya the same page says: they killed her. A footnote reports that Ammar told the Prophet ﷺ the torment had reached its limit, and that the Prophet ﷺ told him to be patient, called him Abu al-Yaqzan, and prayed that none of Ammar's family be punished with the Fire. The Qur'an speaks of the one who is forced to speak words of unbelief while his heart is secure in faith: 'except for one who is forced [to renounce his religion] while his heart is secure in faith' (16:106); the sources read for this chapter do not say that the verse was revealed about Ammar. Ali reports that when Ammar asked permission to enter, the Prophet ﷺ said to let him in, greeting him as the pure one, the purified (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3798 — hasan, Darussalam). Abu Sa'id reports that while the companions built the Prophet's ﷺ mosque, carrying one brick at a time, Ammar carried two; the Prophet ﷺ wiped the dust from his head and said a rebellious group would kill him (Sahih al-Bukhari 2812). How that saying applies to later events is a matter scholars have discussed.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Ammar's family was told to be patient and promised Paradise. What do you hold onto when patience is all you have?

title: Abu Hurayrah
subtitle: The keeper of the Prophet's ﷺ words — who stayed close, hungry, to learn
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 7324 — Abu Hurayrah's hunger
Sahih al-Bukhari 118 — Abu Hurayrah on why he narrated so much

chapters.heading: Hunger and Memory
chapters.body: Abu Hurayrah told of a day of hunger: he fell senseless between the Prophet's ﷺ pulpit and Aisha's room, and a passer-by stepped on his neck and took him for mad — but he had no madness, only hunger (Sahih al-Bukhari 7324). When people said he narrated too much, he answered that were it not for two verses of the Qur'an (2:159-160) he would not have narrated a single hadith; that the Muhajirun were busy with trade in the markets and the Ansar with their property; and that he himself stayed close to the Prophet ﷺ, content with what would fill his stomach, present at what they missed and memorising what they did not (Sahih al-Bukhari 118).

familyQuestion: Abu Hurayrah's poverty became the ummah's library. What is your limitation that could become your offering?

title: Anas ibn Malik
subtitle: The Prophet's ﷺ attendant for ten years — 'he was kind to me'
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 6038 — Anas: ten years of service, he never said 'uff' to me
Sahih al-Bukhari 2893 — Abu Talha takes a boy to serve the Prophet ﷺ at Khaybar

chapters.heading: Ten Years Without 'Uff'
chapters.body: Anas served the Prophet ﷺ for ten years. He said that in all that time the Prophet ﷺ never said even “uff” to him, never asked of anything he had done, why did you do that, and never asked of anything he had not done, why did you not do that (Sahih al-Bukhari 6038). Anas's service began when the Prophet ﷺ asked Abu Talha to choose one of his boys to serve him on the Khaybar expedition; he is described as a boy nearing puberty (Sahih al-Bukhari 2893).

familyQuestion: Ten years of service without one harsh word. What would change in your home if 'uff' disappeared for ten days?

title: Abdullah ibn Abbas
subtitle: The cousin the Prophet ﷺ made dua for — for understanding of the religion and knowledge of the Book
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 75 — the Prophet's ﷺ embrace of Ibn Abbas and dua for knowledge of the Book
Sahih al-Bukhari 143 — the Prophet's ﷺ dua for his understanding of the religion
Sahih al-Bukhari 4970 — Umar and the elders of Badr (Ibn Abbas)

chapters.heading: The Cousin Allah Taught
chapters.body: Ibn Abbas was a boy near the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet ﷺ made dua for him: that Allah give him understanding of the religion (Sahih al-Bukhari 143) and knowledge of the Book (Sahih al-Bukhari 75). Years later some of the elders of Badr who sat with Umar objected: why do you bring this boy to sit with us? Umar answered that it was because of his religious knowledge, then asked them about Surat an-Nasr; Ibn Abbas explained it as a sign of the Prophet's ﷺ approaching death, and Umar said he knew nothing about it beyond that (Sahih al-Bukhari 4970).

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ prayed for a boy's understanding and a library was born. Whose potential could your dua unlock?

title: Mu'adh ibn Jabal
subtitle: The scholar of Yemen — 'you are going to a people of the Book'
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 2 p. 590 (shamela.ws/book/23833/1327)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1327 — the order of the judge: the Book, the sunnah, then one's own reasoning (daʿif — Darussalam)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3790 — the Prophet's ﷺ praise of Mu'adh's knowledge of the lawful and unlawful (sahih — Darussalam)

chapters.heading: The Judge Who Took Revelation With Him
chapters.body: In a report in Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1327 (graded daʿif by Darussalam) the Prophet ﷺ sent Mu'adh to Yemen and asked how he would judge: by the Book of Allah, then by the sunnah, then by his own striving. That report is graded weak (daʿif — Darussalam) because it comes from unnamed companions of Mu'adh, so it is told here as a report, not as established. Ibn Hisham records the Prophet's ﷺ advice to Mu'adh when he sent him to Yemen: make things easy and not hard, give good news and do not drive people away; he would meet People of the Book who would ask for the key to Paradise, and his answer should be the testimony that there is no god but Allah alone, with no partner. The Prophet ﷺ named Mu'adh the most knowledgeable of the ummah about the lawful and the unlawful (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3790 — sahih, Darussalam).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Mu'adh was told: judge by the Book, then the sunnah, then your honest striving. What decision are you avoiding that honest striving would settle?

title: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman
subtitle: The scout of the Trench night — and the son who forgave those who killed his father
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 2 p. 87 (shamela.ws/book/23833/824)
Sahih Muslim 1788 — Hudhayfah sent to scout the enemy on the night of the Trench
Sahih Muslim 2779 — Hudhayfah: twelve hypocrites among the companions

chapters.heading: Sent Into the Night
chapters.body: Ibn Hisham reports that Hudhayfah's father, al-Yaman, a very old man, was killed by mistake by Muslims at Uhud, and that Hudhayfah forgave them. On the night of the Trench the Prophet ﷺ asked for someone to bring news of the enemy; when no one volunteered he called Hudhayfah by name. Hudhayfah went in a harsh wind and cold and found Abu Sufyan warming himself at a fire; he drew an arrow to shoot him but held back, remembering the Prophet's ﷺ order not to provoke the enemy. He returned with the news, and the Prophet ﷺ wrapped him in a spare cloak until morning (Sahih Muslim 1788). Hudhayfah also narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said there would be twelve hypocrites among his companions, eight of whom would not enter Paradise (Sahih Muslim 2779).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Hudhayfah forgave those who killed his father by mistake. What could you forgive today?

title: Khabbab ibn al-Aratt
subtitle: The companion who asked the Prophet ﷺ for help — and was told: be patient
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3612 — his complaint and the Prophet's ﷺ answer

chapters.heading: The Iron and the Answer
chapters.body: Khabbab ibn al-Aratt reported that the Muslims, under persecution, came to the Prophet ﷺ while he was resting on his cloak in the shade of the Kaaba and asked: will you not ask Allah for help for us? He answered that among those before them a man would be seized and sawn in two, or have his flesh combed from his bones with iron combs, and that would not turn him from his religion; and that Allah would complete this matter until a rider travels from Sana'a to Hadramawt fearing none but Allah, and the wolf for his sheep — but you are hasty (Sahih al-Bukhari 3612).

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ promised relief in a generation, not a moment. What long game are you quitting too early?

title: Suhayb ar-Rumi
subtitle: The Byzantine who bought his own life from Quraysh — and laughed last
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — the bargain at the gate of Makkah

chapters.heading: Everything I Own for Myself
chapters.body: He was born to Byzantine parents, captured as a boy, sold in Arabia, and won his own freedom by craft — an archer, a merchant, and a polyglot who had lived inside three civilizations before he ever heard the Qur'an. When he embraced Islam, Quraysh blocked his emigration as they blocked the rest, and as he stood at the gate of Makkah with everything he owned loaded, they said: you came to us a penniless boy and grew rich among us — you go with your religion only if you leave your wealth. Suhayb emptied his caravan into their hands and walked north, and the early sources relate that the Prophet ﷺ, hearing it, said the trade was profitable (seerah report; not from the six books). At Badr he fought; at Uhud he fought; and the reports say that when Umar was stabbed he appointed Suhayb to lead the prayers until the council chose a successor (history; not checked here). The boy Byzantium lost, Arabia enslaved, and Makkah robbed led the prayers in a dark hour, and died in Madinah in the later years of the Rashidun, according to the histories.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Suhayb traded everything visible for everything real. What 'everything' are you holding that you know is worth less than what it costs?

title: Mus'ab ibn Umair
subtitle: The Prophet's ﷺ first envoy to Madinah
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 1 pp. 434-437 (shamela.ws/book/23833/457-460); vol. 2 p. 122 (shamela.ws/book/23833/859)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1276 — Mus'ab shrouded in a single short cloak (Khabbab)

chapters.heading: The First Ambassador to Madinah
chapters.body: Ibn Hisham tells that after the First Pledge of Aqaba the Prophet ﷺ sent Mus'ab ibn Umayr with the delegation to teach them the Qur'an, Islam and the understanding of the religion; he was known in Madinah as the reciter, and stayed in the house of As'ad ibn Zurara. Usayd ibn Hudayr came to confront him, heard Mus'ab speak and recite, and became Muslim. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh then became Muslim at the hands of Mus'ab and As'ad, prayed two rak'as, and told Banu Abd al-Ashhal that he would not speak to their men or women until they believed; by evening, the text says, no man or woman of Banu Abd al-Ashhal was left unbelieving. Mus'ab is listed among the martyrs of Uhud, killed by Ibn Qami'a al-Laythi. Khabbab said Mus'ab was killed at Uhud and left only one cloak, too short to cover both his head and his feet; the Prophet ﷺ ordered his head covered and idhkhir, a shrub, laid over his feet (Sahih al-Bukhari 1276).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Mus'ab was sent to teach a city and was shrouded in a single short cloak. What would you give to carry what you know to others?

title: Abdullah ibn Umar
subtitle: The pilgrim of the ummah — a careful follower of the sunnah
sources: No hadith citation: biographical summary — Not yet scholar-reviewed

chapters.heading: The Man Who Heard and Held
chapters.body: He was the son of the caliph and could have been a king; instead he became the most careful listener the ummah ever produced. The sources remember him as a careful follower of what he heard from the Prophet ﷺ (this chapter is a reflection; the particular anecdotes it once told had no source and are not repeated). The son of the strongest man became the gentlest of the strict.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: One heard prohibition held for a lifetime, at the cost of profit. What principle do you bend the moment it costs you?

title: Ubayy ibn Ka'b
subtitle: The master reciter — named by the Prophet ﷺ among those to learn the Qur'an from
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 4959 — 'Allah has ordered me to recite to you' (Anas)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3808 — take the Qur'an from four, among them Ubayy ibn Ka'b
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3790 — Ubayy the best reciter (sahih — Darussalam)

chapters.heading: The Man Who Learned Directly
chapters.body: Anas reports that the Prophet ﷺ told Ubayy ibn Ka'b that Allah had ordered him to recite Surat al-Bayyina to him. Ubayy asked whether Allah had named him; when the Prophet ﷺ said yes, Ubayy wept (Sahih al-Bukhari 4959). The Prophet ﷺ also named Ubayy among the four to take the Qur'an from (Sahih al-Bukhari 3808), and said Ubayy was the best reciter of the Qur'an among his companions (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3790 — sahih, Darussalam).

familyQuestion: Ubayy knew himself better than his flatterers did. When did you last audit yourself against your own praise?

title: Abu Dharr al-Ghifari
subtitle: The lone voice — who settled at ar-Rabadha
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3522 — Abu Dharr's conversion (Ibn Abbas)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1406 — Abu Dharr at ar-Rabadha (Zayd ibn Wahb)
Sahih Muslim 55 — 'the religion is sincerity' (narrated by Tamim al-Dari)

chapters.heading: The Ascetic Who Learned the Middle
chapters.body: Ibn Abbas told how Abu Dharr, of the tribe of Ghifar, heard that a man in Makkah claimed to be a prophet. He sent his brother to find out; the report did not satisfy him, so he went himself. Ali met him there and brought him to the Prophet ﷺ, and he accepted Islam. The Prophet ﷺ told him to keep it private and go home; instead he declared his faith in the mosque and was beaten, and al-Abbas shielded him on two successive days (Sahih al-Bukhari 3522). Years later Zayd ibn Wahb met him at ar-Rabadha. Abu Dharr said he had disagreed with Mu'awiya in Syria over the verse about those who hoard gold and silver (9:34): Mu'awiya said it concerned the People of the Scripture, Abu Dharr that it included Muslims. Mu'awiya complained to Uthman, who summoned him to Madinah; so many people gathered around him that Uthman offered him a place nearby, and that is how he came to settle at ar-Rabadha. He added that he would obey even an Ethiopian appointed over him (Sahih al-Bukhari 1406). The Prophet ﷺ taught that the religion is sincerity — to Allah, His Book, His Messenger, the leaders of the Muslims and their common people (Sahih Muslim 55, narrated by Tamim al-Dari).

familyQuestion: Abu Dharr chose exile over silence. When is speaking up worth losing everything — and when is the middle the braver place?

title: The Third in the Cave
subtitle: Two men hid in a cave while the hunters stood at the entrance — and Allah was the third
sources: Qur'an 9:40
Sahih al-Bukhari 3653
Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 1 pp. 485-486 (shamela.ws/book/23833/508-509)

chapters.heading: The Hunt at the Threshold
chapters.body: On the night of the Hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr hid in the cave of Thawr while the bounty-hunters stood so close that Abu Bakr whispered that if one of them looked down he would see them. 'O Abu Bakr, what do you think of two whose third is Allah?' the Prophet answered (Bukhari 3653) — the Qur'an preserves the same calm: 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us' (9:40). The most documented hiding place in history, and the hunted man spent his fear on his companion's comfort.

chapters.heading: The Web Added by Later Tradition
chapters.body: Later tradition adds that a spider had woven its web at the entrance and a dove had nested there. Ibn Hisham's account of the cave (it names the cave of Thawr, Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr bringing news at nightfall, Amir ibn Fuhayra's sheep, the three days, the hundred camels offered for the Prophet ﷺ, and Asma bringing food) does not mention a spider or a dove, and neither does the Qur'an (9:40) or Sahih al-Bukhari 3653; no chain for the detail was found. Whatever one holds of that detail, the Qur'an's verdict stands untouched: 'If you do not aid the Prophet - Allah has already aided him when those who disbelieved had driven him out [of Makkah] as one of two, when they were in the cave and he said to his companion, Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us' (9:40). The aid arrived before the help did.
chapters.label: Seerah report

chapters.heading: What the Cave Decided
chapters.body: A spider's thread is not a strategy. Two men and a God are not an army. Yet Madinah was built from that cave, and from Madinah the world changed. The lesson the cave teaches is not that danger is unreal — it is that companionship with Allah reframes the arithmetic of odds. Abu Bakr's rank of as-Siddiq was sealed before any battle was won: he believed in the cave, at the hour when belief was only a voice in the dark.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: Where is our 'cave' right now — and who is our third?
